3.text: among the Maritime Chukchee, and some of them at least were probably

4.text: taken from the Eskimo; for instance, Čeˊple (Chukchee), Čaˊplak (Eskimo).

5.text: The identical form of this name appears, however, also among the Koryak.

6.text: On the other hand, many of the Chukchee names are assumed by the

10.text: Pet names and nicknames are used freely among the Chukchee, some

11.text: of them being quite obscene; such as, Loloˊqai (“little penis”), Rɪh-ñoˊiñɪn

12.text: (“hairy anus”). Others refer to some notorious act of the person designated.

13.text: I have already mentioned the names of Knee-Walker and Necklaced Latuˊwg̣ê.¹

14.text: One man had the very suggestive name of Complete-Liar; another, of

15.text: Separate-Soup-Eater, etc. A man of my acquaintance was nicknamed Frozen-

16.text: Carcass; because, several years before, he had stolen the frozen carcass of

17.text: a reindeer; another, who stole a steel trap, was called Trap. Sometimes,

18.text: at first, the nicknamed persons take offence at being thus named; but such

19.text: an epithet takes root gradually, and finally supersedes the original name.

20.text: Thus the majority of the persons mentioned had discarded their name received

21.text: at birth, and gave the derisive appellation as their only name.

22.text: Pet names given in infancy cling with especial tenacity to their possessors.

23.text: Some of them — such as Loˊlo (“penis”), Loloˊqai (“little penis”) — become

24.text: real names, which are given after the divinatory process.

25.text: The name of the father is sometimes added to the name of the son,

26.text: thus forming the beginning of the family name. Instances of this are found

27.text: in Kokoˊlê-Yaˊtirg̣ɪn, that is, Yaˊtirg̣ɪ̂n, son of Kukuˊli; Tatk-omruˊwg̣ê, that

28.text: is, Omruˊwg̣ê, son of Taˊtko; etc. Less frequently the wife assumes the name

29.text: of her husband; for example, Notaiˊmê-ñaw, the wife of Notaiˊmen. Regarding
